newsitem.title: USA: CME live, feeder cattle end up, feeders post highs.
newsitem.headline: CME live, feeder cattle end up, feeders post highs.

text.p: Falling feed costs sparked demand in CME feeder cattle futures and all contracts from November and beyond climbed to contract highs by the close, traders said. Short covering and technical support also lifted live cattle for gains, traders said.

Feeder cattle closed 0.150 to 0.750 cent per lb higher with August up 0.300 at 78.600 cents. November through May posted new contract highs. Live cattle finished 0.400 to 0.125 cent per lb higher with August up most at 63.775 cents.
Corn futures fell to new contract lows which, along with tight feeder supplies, buoyed feeder contracts to new highs, traders said.

"You just continue to hear that it is hard to find feeders for this fall because the greatest majority of them are contracted already - so the cash (feeder) market is going to be rather tight if you need to do some outright pruchasing," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
The latest CME feeder cattle index was up $0.59 at $77.56 per cwt, a new high for the move and highest price level since August 18, 1994.
Cargill Investor Services was a notable buyer in all months. Dean Witter and E.D.&F. Man also bought August while ABN Chicogo Corp and Smith Barney sold September during the day, pit sources said.

Trading turned mostly technical in live cattle as futures held support and moved up to resistance. Futures ran up early to resistance on commercial hedge lifting but drifted down for losses before bouncing at chart support. Strength came despite further pressure in cash markets, traders said.
Support in August at around 63.100 dates back to January, chartists said.

R.J. O'Brien bought August early while Refco, Prudential Securities, E.D.&F. Man and Cargill bought late. In live cattle options, commercials did risk reversals in December, buying 68 puts and selling 72 calls and commission houses bought August 67 and 68 calls early, pit sources said.

Boneless beef pared losses and trimmings finished mostly higher as speculative short covering developed. Both contracts had retreated early on concern over compitition from lower priced chuck meat but persistant commercial buying in October trimmings turned futures back up, traders said.

Pit sources noted early pressure following reports that 40 loads of chucks traded seven cents lower on Tuesday. Expectations were that this would take demand away from boneless beef and trimmings and futures fell early before meeting the commercial support, they said.
Boneless beef closed 0.90 to 0.80 cent per lb lower with August off most at 93.90 cents. Trimmings ended 0.40 lower to 0.10 higher with only August off at 42.00 cents.
